text: The *bnei elohim* ("sons of God") in Genesis 6 have one of the strangest reception histories of any passage in the Bible. The Book of Enoch is an ancient Jewish work preserved most fully in Ethiopic versions, and the Ethiopian Orthodox Church reads it as scripture. Enoch elaborated a tradition of fallen angels, the Watchers, who came down and corrupted humanity in two ways: by forbidden teaching and by miscegenation. Jude 6 and 2 Peter 2:4 may presuppose this angelic reading. Augustine rejected it in *City of God*. He preferred the Sethite account, in which the sons of God are the godly line of Seth and the daughters of men belong to the line of Cain. Other readers have compared the passage with ancient Near Eastern traditions in which kings and other powerful men claimed descent from gods. The chapter also introduces the flood narrative, and that story belongs to a broader Mesopotamian tradition, preserved most fully in the *Atrahasis* epic and in tablet XI of the *Epic of Gilgamesh* (the Utnapishtim narrative). Both texts contain close parallels to the biblical flood story. Noah's vessel has its own echo elsewhere in Scripture. The Hebrew word for it, *tevah* ("ark," "chest"), appears in only one other place, for the basket in which the infant Moses is set adrift on the Nile.
